chief_complaint: recurrent ear infections and severe pneumonias since turning 6 months old
hpi_details: 10-month-old male presenting with his fourth episode of Streptococcus pneumoniae pneumonia and chronic otitis media. The mother notes he was completely healthy until about 6 months of age, at which point he started getting sick constantly. He has two healthy older sisters, but a maternal uncle died of severe pneumonia in infancy.
ideas: mother thinks his immune system is just immature
concerns: worried he will end up like her brother who passed away
expectations: wants strong antibiotics and tests for his immune system

investigation_events.title: Quantitative immunoglobulins and B-cell count
investigation_events.availability_message: The immunoglobulin levels and B-cell count are now available.

core_concepts: XLA is caused by a BTK gene mutation leading to failure of B-cell maturation, very low or absent circulating B cells, and markedly reduced immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE).
Infants are protected by maternal IgG for the first ~6 months, leading to a classic presentation of recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections starting between 6-9 months of age.
Treatment involves lifelong Intravenous/Subcutaneous Immunoglobulin (IVIG/SCIG) replacement.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: recurrent ear infections and severe pneumonias since turning 6 months old
Key HPI features: Male infant, asymptomatic first 6 months, then recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections. Maternal family history of early male infant death.
Objective/Exam findings: Absent or very small tonsils and lymph nodes.
common_misconceptions: Confusing XLA with SCID; XLA patients have normal T-cell function and combat viral/fungal infections normally (except enteroviruses).
Assuming recurrent ear infections in a baby are always just normal daycare exposures.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize the X-linked inheritance pattern and offer genetic counseling and carrier testing to at-risk relatives.
Administering live polio vaccine (though rare now) which can cause vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis in XLA.
management_principles: Aggressive antibiotic therapy for acute infections.
Initiate lifelong IVIG or SCIG replacement therapy.
Avoid live enteroviral vaccines (especially oral polio vaccine); obtain immunology guidance for vaccination planning.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 10-month-old male presenting with 4th pneumonia. Healthy until 6 months of age. Maternal uncle died of pneumonia in infancy.
reference_soap.objective: Fever 39.0C. Diminished breath sounds right lower lobe. Absent tonsils and cervical lymph nodes on exam.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Treat acute pneumonia with IV Ceftriaxone. 2. Quantitative immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE) and flow cytometry for B-cell count (CD19+). 3. Refer to Pediatric Immunology for lifelong IVIG therapy initiation and genetic testing for BTK mutation.

learning_objectives: Identify the classic 6-month onset window for XLA due to waning maternal IgG
Recognize the X-linked inheritance pattern (maternal male relatives affected)
Understand that B-cells and immunoglobulins are completely absent, requiring IVIG

teaching.one_liner: A genetic defect in males preventing B-cell development, leading to severe bacterial infections that start at 6 months when maternal antibodies fade.
differentials: Common Variable Immunodeficiency (usually presents later in life)
red_flags: Family history of infant male deaths from infection

must_ask.say: Was he completely healthy for the first few months of his life?

must_ask.objective: Determine family history indicating X-linked trait
must_ask.say: Are there any males on the mother's side of the family who had severe infections or died young?
What kind of infections does he mostly get? Are they mainly ear, sinus, and lung infections?

history.answer: My 10-month-old son has been suffering from back-to-back ear infections and lung infections, and now his high fever and chest cough have returned.
His current fever and wet cough began two days ago, but his repeated infections started right around six months of age.
The chest congestion is deep in his lungs, and he constantly rubs and pulls at his right ear.
He has a heavy, rattling cough and fast breathing, and he cries frequently because his ear seems to hurt.
This is his fourth episode of pneumonia in four months, and his middle ear fluid never seems to clear up completely.
His coughing worsens whenever he lies down flat, and fever medicines only lower his temperature for about an hour or two.
He has a thick yellowish nasal discharge and decreased appetite, but he has had no vomiting, diarrhea, or skin rashes.
His temperature reached 39 degrees Celsius today and his breathing is rapid, but he is still drinking small sips and waking up.
He was hospitalized three times previously for severe pneumonia and required intravenous antibiotics each time.
Our pediatrician started him on oral amoxicillin-clavulanate three days ago, but his fever and coughing have only gotten worse.
He stays home with me every day, has had no contact with sick individuals, and has not traveled anywhere.
He cannot sleep through the night because the coughing keeps waking him up, and he refuses all solid baby food.
He was completely healthy and never caught a single illness during his first six months, but since turning six months old he has been sick nonstop.
Every serious illness has been in his lungs or his ears; he has never had persistent oral thrush, unusual skin boils, or chronic diarrhea.
I was hoping his immune system was simply immature and needed a little more time to catch up.
I am terrified that he has the same condition that caused my baby brother to die of a severe lung infection in infancy.
I want his immune system thoroughly tested and hope he can receive stronger antibiotics to get him through this safely.
Aside from recurrent otitis media and recurrent pneumonias starting at six months old, he has no other chronic medical conditions.
He has never undergone any surgical procedures.
He is currently taking amoxicillin-clavulanate oral suspension twice daily, as well as infant acetaminophen syrup for fever.
He has no known allergies to medications, foods, or environmental triggers.
My two older daughters are completely healthy, but my younger brother died of a severe lung infection when he was an infant.
He lives in an apartment with my husband, our two older daughters, and me; no one smokes in our household.
He was born at 39 weeks by an uncomplicated vaginal delivery, weighing 3.4 kilograms.
He has been growing steadily along the 50th percentile, sits up without support, and babbles normally.
He has received all routine childhood vaccinations on schedule, including his pneumococcal shots, with no adverse reactions.
He does not attend daycare and stays home with me, so he has not been exposed to sick children.

exam.finding: Temperature 39.0°C, heart rate 146 bpm, respiratory rate 46 breaths/min, blood pressure 90/55 mmHg, oxygen saturation 95% on room air.
Irritable, flushed male infant in mild respiratory distress with mild subcostal retractions and nasal flaring, resting in his mother's arms.
Right tympanic membrane is erythematous, cloudy, and bulging with decreased mobility; left tympanic membrane is dull without perforation.
Mucopurulent secretions in anterior nares; oral pharynx mildly injected; palatine tonsils are notably absent on inspection.
No palpable cervical or submandibular lymphadenopathy; lymphoid tissue in anterior and posterior cervical chains is noticeably absent.
Diminished breath sounds and coarse inspiratory crackles over the right lower lung base; no wheezing or stridor.
Tachycardic, regular rhythm; normal S1 and S2 with no audible heart murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Abdomen is soft, flat, and non-tender to light and deep palpation without guarding or rigidity.
Liver edge is smooth and palpable 1 cm below the right costal margin; spleen is not palpable.
Warm and flushed skin without petechiae, purpura, eczema, or active cutaneous abscesses.
Length and body weight track along the 50th percentile; age-appropriate gross motor milestones and social interactions noted.
